title: Good for some, bad for others

files.lesson.md:
---
order: 3
unit: water
title: Good for some, bad for others
node: AC9HG7K01 n3
summary: "When water moves from one place to another, it changes things in both places. Those changes are its effects. Some effects help people or the environment and some harm them, and the same change can help one group and harm another. Geographers often sort effects into environmental, economic and social ones, though a single change can fit more than one. This lesson looks at the Snowy Mountains scheme and made-up cases to see who gains and who loses when water is moved."
language: maths
hook: If water is moved to help one place, does every connected place benefit?
explainPicture: { ref: boards.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Kerrin is made up. The dam holds back soil and evens out the town's water, and less water and soil reach the lake." }
---
Moving water can have **environmental effects** on habitats, plants, animals and water quality; **economic effects** on production, jobs and income; and **social effects** on daily life, access and recreation. An **effect** says what changes because water moves. “The channel is long” is a description, not an effect.

These categories are lenses. A change can fit more than one; explain which part you mean.

## Predict: who benefits?

```step
stage: predict
insight: Question whether a helpful connection helps everyone.
check:
  type: predict
  q: In a made-up valley, a channel takes water to crops but leaves less flowing to a wetland. What is most
    likely?
  options:
    - It can help farmers and harm wetland habitat
    - Every connected place must benefit equally
    - The water cannot affect anything outside the farms
    - The channel’s size is the only thing that matters
  actual: One change can help crop production and reduce water reaching wetland habitat. Benefits depend on the
    place or group.
```

## Try: what kind of effect?

```step
stage: run
insight: Sort effects by what changes and reject a non-effect.
check:
  type: sort
  q: In this made-up valley, sort each statement by its main focus.
  options:
    - Environmental
    - Economic
    - Social
    - Description, not an effect
  items:
    - - Less water reaches wetland plants
      - Environmental
      - This focuses on habitat conditions.
    - - Farmers can grow crops for sale
      - Economic
      - This focuses on production and income.
    - - Families lose access to a swimming spot
      - Social
      - This focuses on daily life and recreation.
    - - The channel is long
      - Description, not an effect
      - Length alone does not explain a consequence.
```

## Worked example: the Snowy connection

```step
stage: investigate
insight: Use an Australian example to link movement and consequence.
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: According to the real-place card, what is one economic effect of the Snowy Scheme’s water movement?
      options:
        - Diverted water supplies irrigation for farms downstream
        - Changed river flow alters conditions in the river channel
        - Water moves west through tunnels into other river systems
        - The scheme collects and stores water in its dams
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - This focuses on environmental conditions rather than production or income.
        - This describes a pathway without an economic consequence.
        - This describes operation without an economic consequence.
      explain: Diversion inland supplies irrigation that supports crop production.
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: working.txt#nib
      text: Nib explains the case. Click the first line where the reasoning goes wrong.
      answer: 2
      fault: logic
      misconception: water-benefits-everyone
      explain: Line 2 turns one benefit into a benefit for every place. The same diversion can help one place and
        harm another.
    smaller:
      check:
        type: question
        q: A made-up channel sends more water to crops and less to a wetland. Which receives less?
        options:
          - The wetland
          - The crops
        answer: 0
        feedback:
          - null
          - The case says more water reaches the crops.
        explain: Different places can experience different effects from the same movement.
```

### One real change, different effects

```worked
\text{Movement} :: The Snowy Scheme diverts water west into the Murray and Murrumbidgee for irrigation.
\text{Consequence} :: Irrigation supplies water to crops.
\text{Effect} :: Supporting crop production is an economic effect.
```

The **Snowy Mountains Scheme** collects, stores and diverts water westward through tunnels and hydro-electric power stations into the **Murray and Murrumbidgee rivers**, for town water supplies, irrigation and the environment. It also generates hydro-electric power.

*Source: [Moving water through the Snowy Scheme (Snowy Hydro fact sheet)](https://www.snowyhydro.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/3-Moving-water-thru-SS_Water-scheme-Factsheet.pdf), checked 1 November 2026.*

NSW Environment and Heritage describes how flows in the Snowy River below **Jindabyne Dam** were cut to a tiny share of their usual amount for decades, and how the river channel changed greatly. Environmental releases now flush sediment out to help reclaim a deeper channel. This is an environmental consequence alongside the economic uses.

*Source: [Managing water for the environment: Snowy and montane rivers (NSW Environment and Heritage)](https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/topics/water/water-for-the-environment/catchments/snowy-and-montane/managing), checked 1 November 2026.*

### Find Nib’s slip



## Vary: explain the effect

```step
stage: modify
insight: Separate description from explanation and compare consequences.
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: Which sentence explains an effect of moving water?
      options:
        - Diversion supplies irrigation, supporting crop production
        - The Snowy Scheme collects and stores water in its dams
        - The Murray and Murrumbidgee are both named river systems
        - The scheme has structures that help it move water inland
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - This describes operation; add what changes because of it.
        - Names alone do not explain a consequence.
        - Structures describe how it works; add what changes for a place or group.
      explain: The explanation links movement to production.
  - check:
      type: question
      q: Imagine a made-up town where diversion improves farm supply but leaves a swimming area too shallow. Which
        comparison fits?
      options:
        - Economic benefit for farms; social harm for swimmers
        - Economic benefit for all; social benefit for swimmers
        - Environmental benefit for all; no changes to daily life
        - Social harm for farmers; economic harm for swimmers
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - The case says swimmers lose access.
        - A swimming area becoming unusable is a change to daily life.
        - "That swaps them: the farms gain water (economic) and the swimmers lose access (social)."
      explain: The same diversion affects groups differently.
```

### A made-up contrast



## Try it on the board: add a dam

```step
stage: modify
insight: One change on a river can help one place and take something from another.
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#dam", height: 680 }
tasks:
  - check:
      type: board
      text: "Send a storm with no dam first. Then add the dam and send another storm. Compare the town and the lake."
      when: "dam_compared = 1 and dam_on = 1 and n_storms >= 1"
    hint:
      - Send one storm as it is, and read the list under the buttons.
      - Choose Dam, then send another storm.
      - Compare the lines for the town and the lake with your first storm.
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: The dam in Kerrin is made up. Sort what changed by its main focus.
      options:
        - Environmental
        - Economic
        - Social
        - Description, not an effect
      items:
        - - Less water and soil reach the lake
          - Environmental
          - This is about the lake and the plants and animals that live there.
        - - Town businesses can count on a steadier water supply
          - Economic
          - This is about work and income.
        - - Families in town see less muddy water in their river
          - Social
          - This is about daily life by the river.
        - - The dam sits on the river above the town
          - Description, not an effect
          - Where the dam is does not say what changed.
  - check:
      type: question
      q: Nib says, “The dam made more water for Kerrin, so every place downstream gets more.” What does the board show?
      options:
        - The dam holds back the same storm's water, so less goes on to the lake
        - The dam made extra water, so the lake gets more too
        - Nothing below the dam changes
        - Only the town is affected by the dam
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - A dam stores and releases water. It does not make rain.
        - That ignores the lake. With the dam, less water and soil reached it.
        - The lake is downstream of the town. What reached it?
      explain: A dam can help the town and leave the lake with less water and soil. Both effects are real.
      fault: logic
      misconception: dam-creates-water
```

### Storm, then dam

The board is a simple made-up model: it shows which way things change, not real amounts. Real dams also release water on purpose, which this board leaves out.

## Practise: cause to consequence

```step
stage: practise
insight: Identify an effect and explain why one benefit does not cancel a harm.
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: Match the made-up effect to the focus in the sentence.
      pairs:
        - - Floodwater damages nesting habitat
          - Environmental harm
        - - Reliable irrigation raises farm output
          - Economic benefit
        - - Cleaner creek water lets families use a picnic area again
          - Social benefit
      explain: Another category can fit if you explain your focus.
  - check:
      type: question
      q: A made-up channel raises crop output and reduces water reaching a marsh. Which conclusion is supported?
      options:
        - The crop benefit and habitat harm can both be real
        - More crops prove that marsh habitat has improved
        - Marsh damage proves the crops receive no benefit
        - There are no effects because the water still exists
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - Production does not prove habitat has improved.
        - An adverse effect does not erase a separate benefit.
        - Where water reaches and what changes there matter.
      explain: Judge each consequence for the affected place or group.
```

### Can both be true?



## Make: one effect with a reason

```step
stage: make
insight: Explain one effect type and recognise contrasting consequences.
check:
  type: reflect
  text: In my own book I explained one effect of the Snowy Scheme’s water movement using the card and a because
    link. I named a benefit and an adverse effect of the same movement. A partner or teacher read it.
```

Choose an environmental or economic effect from the cards. Name where water moves and what changes because of it. Add the contrasting benefit or harm. You do not need all three categories to finish. Write in your book, not on this page.

## Typical: three lenses, two cases

```step
stage: make
insight: Widen to all lenses across cases.
check:
  type: reflect
  text: In my book I used all three lenses across the Snowy cards and the made-up farm-and-swimming-town case,
    explaining which groups gain or lose.
tier: typical
```

Use only the stated case details. The made-up case supplies a social effect; do not invent an actual community’s experience of the Snowy Scheme.

## Wider: change the viewpoint

```step
stage: make
insight: Test how the affected group changes the judgement.
check:
  type: reflect
  text: For the made-up diversion I wrote a farmer’s reason for supporting it and a swimmer’s or habitat carer’s
    reason for concern. Each names the water connection.
tier: wider
```

Explain both viewpoints before naming information you would want next.

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
summary: Students explain an effect of moving water as a change, not a
  description, and see that one change can benefit some people and places and
  harm others. They sort effects as environmental, economic or social, treating
  these as lenses that can overlap. The worked example is the Snowy Mountains
  scheme; the other cases are made up.
learning: explain an effect of moving water and show how it can benefit some
  places or groups and harm others
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 8 min · Practise 6
  min · Make 6 min. Optional width is extra.
goals:
  - I can explain one effect of water movement using a specific example.
  - I can distinguish environmental, economic and social effects.
  - I can identify a benefit and an adverse effect of the same movement.
struggle: Students may label an effect without a causal link. Ask what changed
  because water went somewhere different. Accept justified overlapping
  categories.
before: Usually Year 7. The minimum Make explains one effect type using the
  Snowy Scheme, plus a contrasting benefit and harm. Introducing three lenses in
  a short sort does not require an essay on all three. Real facts are limited to
  the source cards; no current volumes, allocations or particular community
  viewpoints are asserted. Towns, swimming areas and other comparison cases are
  made up. Environmental releases are acknowledged so historic diversion is not
  mistaken for all current operations.
running:
  - "Try: channel length is a description, not a consequence."
  - "Worked example: compare the real economic use with the environmental
    consequence."
  - "Vary: mark the swimming-town case as hypothetical."
  - "Board: one storm without the dam, one with it. Ask who gained and who gave
    something up."
  - "Board: Kerrin and the catchment board are made up. The board is a simple
    model of which way things change, not amounts; it leaves out rain amount and
    intensity, soil type, groundwater, dams releasing or flushing water, and
    change over years. Ask students what a real catchment would add."
  - "Make: expect one explained type; all three remain optional width."
stuck:
  - see: A student gives dam size as an effect.
    ask: What changes because water moves?
    fix: Add a consequence for a place or group.
  - see: One benefit is taken to benefit everyone.
    ask: Where might less water arrive?
    fix: Compare receiving places with places from which flow is diverted.
  - see: Every effect is given exactly one category.
    ask: Which aspect are you focusing on?
    fix: Accept overlapping categories with a reason.
support: "Use the smaller two-place question, then the frame: water moves from
  __ to __, so __ changes."
stretch: Use both viewpoints in the invented case without making up evidence
  about actual communities.
exit:
  q: Explain one effect of the Snowy Scheme and a contrasting consequence.
  a: Diversion supplies water for irrigation, an economic benefit for farms. Much
    lower Snowy River flows changed the channel greatly; environmental releases
    now flush sediment to reclaim a deeper channel.
explain: An effect says what changes because water moves. Environmental focuses
  on nature, economic on production and income, social on daily life. One
  movement can help one place and harm another.
sources:
  - title: Moving water through the Snowy Scheme (Snowy Hydro fact sheet)
    url: https://www.snowyhydro.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/3-Moving-water-thru-SS_Water-scheme-Factsheet.pdf
    checked: 2026-10-30
  - title: "Managing water for the environment: Snowy and montane rivers (NSW
      Environment and Heritage)"
    url: https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/topics/water/water-for-the-environment/catchments/snowy-and-montane/managing
    checked: 2026-10-30
leads: 'Next: the physical processes by which water changes land. First Nations
  extension is teacher-led only. ACARA’s AC9HG7K01 elaboration says: "explaining
  the environmental, economic or social effects of water as it connects places;
  for example, the environmental effects of water diversion in the Snowy
  Mountains, the economic effects of irrigation in the Ord River or the social
  effects of the Mutitjulu Waterhole connecting Australian First Nations Peoples
  in Central Australia". Start from that elaboration and add local,
  community-approved material with the school’s Indigenous education contact. No
  student explanation of First Nations history, culture, values or connection to
  Country is supplied.'
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Does a benefit from moving water make the whole change a good one?
    prompts:
      - What is your reason?
      - What information would change your view?
    notes: Ask good for whom, where and in what way. Keep actual evidence separate
      from hypothetical viewpoints.
  activities:
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: One change, two consequences
      minutes: 5
      do: Pairs use the Snowy cards to name a benefit and an adverse effect of the
        same diversion. Ask which sentence explains a change and which only
        describes the scheme.
      notes: Ask good for whom, where and in what way. Keep actual evidence separate
        from hypothetical viewpoints.
    - at: modify
      kind: discussion
      title: Same storm, with a dam
      minutes: 4
      do: Send one storm without the dam and one with it. Pairs name one gain for the
        town and one loss for the lake.
      notes: Both effects are real; neither cancels the other.
    - at: make
      kind: activity
      title: Compare your explanations
      minutes: 4
      do: Write in your own book, then swap with a partner. The partner identifies the
        geographical terms and one link explained with because.
      notes: The reflect tick records completion. The teacher or partner reads the
        writing; the site does not assess it.
```
